preamble: Spinal Muscular Atrophy  |  SMN1-Related 5q Spinal Muscular Atrophy  |  Werdnig-Hoffmann Disease (Type 1) / Dubowitz Disease (Type 2) / Kugelberg-Welander Disease (Type 3)  (OMIM 253300 / 253550 / 253400)

questions.domain: Onset of hypotonia and weakness before 6 months of age (Type 1)?
questions.question: Yes – Type 1 (most common): onset 0–6 months; Type 2: onset 6–18 months; Type 3: onset after 18 months; onset age is the primary determinant of SMA clinical type classification

questions.domain: Progressive, symmetric proximal > distal limb weakness?
questions.question: Yes – bilateral symmetric proximal muscle weakness is the cardinal feature across all SMA types; lower extremities typically weaker than upper; progression is the rule without disease-modifying treatment

questions.domain: Pure lower motor neuron phenotype — NO upper motor neuron signs (no spasticity, no Babinski)?
questions.question: Yes – SMA is purely a lower motor neuron disease; spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, and Babinski response are absent; their presence should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis

questions.domain: Preserved sensation — intact pinprick, light touch, vibration, and proprioception?
questions.question: Yes – sensory pathways are entirely spared in 5q SMA; normal sensory examination is a clinically important positive finding; any sensory deficit warrants evaluation for hereditary neuropathy

questions.domain: Normal intellect and cognitive development for age (preserved despite severe motor impairment)?
questions.question: Yes – intelligence is characteristically normal in SMA; preserved cognition, social engagement, and language development are distinguishing features from other causes of infantile hypotonia

questions.domain: Positive family history of SMA in a sibling or known carrier parents?
questions.question: Yes – autosomal recessive inheritance; 25% recurrence risk per pregnancy for carrier couple; carrier frequency ~1 in 40–50 in the general population; positive family history in ~30–40% of cases

questions.domain: Marked generalized hypotonia — "floppy infant" presentation?
questions.question: Yes – profound hypotonia is a hallmark of SMA; classical "frog-leg" resting posture in Type 1; reduced but present axial tone in Type 2–3; antigravity movements often absent or reduced

questions.domain: "Frog-leg" resting posture (hips abducted and externally rotated, knees flexed) at rest?
questions.question: Yes – characteristic frog-leg posture reflects proximal lower extremity weakness and hypotonia; pathognomonic for severe infantile hypotonia and highly characteristic of Type 1 SMA

questions.domain: Never achieved sitting independently (Type 1) OR achieved sitting but never walking (Type 2)?
questions.question: Yes – functional motor milestones determine clinical type: Type 1 = non-sitter; Type 2 = sitter but non-stander/non-walker; Type 3 = achieves walking; milestone profile is required for classification

questions.domain: Paradoxical breathing pattern — inward thoracic excursion on inspiration with abdominal rise (bell-shaped chest)?
questions.question: Yes – intercostal muscle weakness with relative diaphragm sparing causes paradoxical breathing and a bell-shaped chest; characteristic of Type 1 and severe Type 2; visible on observation

questions.domain: Visible fasciculations of the tongue?
questions.question: Yes – tongue fasciculations are a highly characteristic lower motor neuron sign in SMA; present in the majority of Type 1–2 patients; best observed with the tongue at rest; pathognomonic in the correct clinical context

questions.domain: Fine postural hand tremor — minipolymyoclonus of outstretched fingers?
questions.question: Yes – fine irregular tremor of the outstretched fingers (minipolymyoclonus) reflects motor unit instability from chronic denervation and reinnervation; characteristic in SMA Type 2–3; supports anterior horn cell disease

questions.domain: Preserved facial expression and eye movements (facial / extraocular muscles spared)?
questions.question: Yes – facial and extraocular muscles are consistently preserved in SMA; intact social smile and eye tracking in Type 1 infants are clinically important and diagnostically useful distinguishing features

sections.heading: REFLEX AND LOWER MOTOR NEURON FINDINGS

questions.domain: Absent or severely reduced deep tendon reflexes (areflexia) on examination?
questions.question: Yes – absent deep tendon reflexes are a cardinal lower motor neuron finding reflecting anterior horn cell depletion; present in virtually all SMA types from early in the disease course

questions.domain: No upper motor neuron signs — no spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, or extensor plantar response?
questions.question: Yes – absence of all UMN signs is required for SMA diagnosis; any UMN sign should prompt evaluation for ALS-overlap syndromes, leukodystrophy, or other CNS pathology

questions.domain: Normal or only mildly elevated serum creatine kinase (CK) — typically <5× ULN?
questions.question: Yes – CK is normal or mildly elevated in SMA (anterior horn cell disease); markedly elevated CK (>5–10× ULN) strongly favors a primary muscle disease such as Duchenne or Becker muscular dystrophy

questions.domain: Respiratory compromise — recurrent aspiration pneumonia, weak cough, or need for ventilatory support?
questions.question: Yes – respiratory failure from intercostal and accessory muscle weakness is the primary cause of mortality in Type 1 and progressive morbidity in Type 2; proactive monitoring and early intervention are life-saving

questions.domain: Forced vital capacity (FVC) reduced — <60% predicted on spirometry or respiratory function testing?
questions.question: Yes – FVC % predicted is the primary respiratory surveillance tool; values below 60% indicate significant restrictive impairment; serial FVC correlates with disease progression and risk of respiratory decompensation

questions.domain: Nocturnal hypoventilation confirmed on overnight oximetry or capnography (elevated CO₂, desaturations)?
questions.question: Yes – nocturnal hypoventilation and sleep-disordered breathing are early indicators of respiratory compromise; overnight oximetry is a first-line, non-invasive surveillance tool; capnography confirms CO₂ retention

questions.domain: Weak or absent cry in infancy?
questions.question: Yes – a weak or absent cry reflects both bulbar and respiratory muscle weakness; typically one of the earliest clinically detected signs in Type 1 SMA; parents reliably report this

questions.domain: Progressive scoliosis developing over time?
questions.question: Yes – scoliosis is nearly universal in SMA Type 2 and non-ambulatory Type 3 due to paraspinal muscle weakness; can cause secondary respiratory compromise; requires annual spinal surveillance from childhood

questions.domain: Hip dislocation, subluxation, or large joint contractures?
questions.question: Yes – hip subluxation/dislocation and joint contractures are common complications of SMA Type 1–2 due to muscle imbalance and positioning; require regular orthopedic and physiotherapy surveillance

questions.domain: Reduced bone mineral density — fragility fractures or osteoporosis?
questions.question: Yes – reduced bone density from immobility and disuse is well-documented in SMA Types 1–2; pathological fractures can occur with minimal trauma; DEXA scanning and calcium/vitamin D optimization required

questions.domain: Bulbar weakness — dysphagia, feeding difficulties, or silent aspiration?
questions.question: Yes – bulbar muscle weakness in Type 1 leads to inability to feed safely; aspiration pneumonia is a major cause of morbidity; videofluoroscopic swallow study (VFSS) is essential for safe feeding assessment

questions.domain: Nasal regurgitation or inability to generate adequate suction for bottle/breastfeeding?
questions.question: Yes – soft palate and pharyngeal weakness causes nasal regurgitation and poor suck in Type 1 infants; contributes to inadequate caloric intake and failure to thrive

questions.domain: Requirement for nasogastric tube (NG) or gastrostomy tube (G-tube) for safe nutrition?
questions.question: Yes – Type 1 SMA infants typically progress from NG to G-tube by 6–9 months; prophylactic G-tube placement is standard of care in Type 1 at many centers, often alongside respiratory interventions

questions.domain: Constipation or abdominal distension from GI dysmotility?
questions.question: Yes – constipation and GI dysmotility are well-recognized in SMA across all types; abdominal muscle weakness contributes; requires active dietary and pharmacological management

questions.domain: Normal cognitive development with intact language, social engagement, and learning?
questions.question: Yes – intellectual ability is fully preserved in 5q SMA; children with Type 1 SMA show age-appropriate social engagement, visual attention, and prelinguistic communication — a striking and diagnostically important contrast with their motor impairment

questions.domain: Normal sensory examination — intact light touch, pinprick, vibration, and proprioception in all limbs?
questions.question: Yes – sensory modalities are entirely spared in SMN1-related SMA; any sensory deficit should prompt evaluation for hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy (HMSN/CMT) or a congenital neuropathy

questions.domain: Preserved eye movements and facial expression (cranial nerves III, IV, VI, VII intact)?
questions.question: Yes – cranial nerves controlling eye movement and facial expression are consistently spared in SMA; preserved facial expressivity and social smile in Type 1 infants is a characteristic and clinically important observation

questions.domain: EMG — widespread chronic and/or active denervation (fibrillations, positive sharp waves, large motor units, reduced recruitment)?
questions.question: Yes – EMG in SMA shows denervation: fibrillation potentials, positive sharp waves, large-amplitude polyphasic MUAPs reflecting reinnervation, and reduced interference pattern; consistent with anterior horn cell loss

questions.domain: Normal motor and sensory nerve conduction velocities (NCS)?
questions.question: Yes – NCS are typically normal in SMA (or show mildly reduced CMAP amplitudes in severe cases); normal conduction velocities distinguish SMA from hereditary motor and sensory neuropathies (CMT types)

questions.domain: Muscle biopsy showing grouped atrophy of angular fibers with type grouping (if performed)?
questions.question: Variable – muscle biopsy is rarely required for diagnosis if SMN1 testing is available; when performed, shows classic denervation: grouped small angular fiber atrophy with type-grouping from reinnervation; hypertrophic type 1 fibers

questions.domain: Positive newborn screening (NBS) result for SMA — SMN1 deletion detected on NBS?
questions.question: Yes – SMA was added to the US RUSP in 2018; NBS detects SMN1 homozygous exon 7 deletion by real-time PCR from dried blood spot; >45 US states and 25+ countries screen; result available day 2–5 of life

questions.domain: Pre-symptomatic identification enabling treatment before motor neuron loss?
questions.question: Yes – treatment initiated within 2–4 weeks of NBS-positive result dramatically improves outcomes; near-normal motor development achieved in many genotypic Type 1 infants treated before symptom onset; urgency is paramount

questions.domain: Autosomal recessive inheritance pattern — both parents confirmed obligate or tested carriers?
questions.question: Yes – SMA is autosomal recessive; carrier frequency ~1/40–50 in the general population; 25% recurrence risk per pregnancy for two carrier parents; ACMG recommends universal carrier screening

questions.domain: Parental SMN1 copy number confirming both parents have one SMN1 copy (carrier status)?
questions.question: Yes – parental SMN1 copy number analysis by MLPA or ddPCR confirms carrier status; note: ~4% of carriers have 2 SMN1 copies on one chromosome (2+0 arrangement) and can be missed by standard dosage assays

questions.domain: Homozygous deletion of SMN1 exon 7 confirmed by MLPA, ddPCR, or next-generation sequencing?
questions.question: Yes – homozygous SMN1 exon 7 deletion is the DEFINITIVE diagnosis in approximately 95% of SMA cases; a single gene test is confirmatory; this result alone is sufficient to establish the diagnosis

questions.domain: SMN2 copy number determined (1, 2, 3, or 4 copies)?
questions.question: Yes – SMN2 copy number is the strongest genetic modifier of SMA severity: 1 copy → Type 0/most severe Type 1; 2 copies → typical Type 1; 3 copies → Type 2; 4 copies → Type 3; critical for prognosis and treatment urgency; typically reported alongside SMN1 analysis

questions.domain: Compound heterozygosity confirmed — one SMN1 deletion allele + one intragenic SMN1 point mutation (for non-deletion cases)?
questions.question: Yes – approximately 5% of SMA patients have a deletion on one SMN1 allele and a pathogenic point mutation on the other; single-allele deletion on standard dosage analysis does NOT exclude SMA — SMN1 sequencing required

questions.domain: No pathogenic DMD variant — Duchenne/Becker muscular dystrophy excluded (serum CK markedly elevated in DMD)?
questions.question: Yes – DMD/BMD excluded: DMD presents with markedly elevated CK (10–100× ULN), proximal weakness + calf pseudohypertrophy, and PRESERVED reflexes early; CK is normal/near-normal in SMA

questions.domain: Infantile-onset Pompe disease excluded — acid alpha-glucosidase enzyme activity normal?
questions.question: Yes – Pompe disease (GSD II) excluded: infantile Pompe causes hypotonia + cardiomegaly + elevated CK; acid glucosidase enzyme assay distinguishes; cardiac involvement absent in SMA; Pompe now on NBS in many states

questions.domain: Congenital myopathies excluded — muscle biopsy or myopathy panel negative (if evaluated)?
questions.question: Yes – congenital myopathies (nemaline, central core, centronuclear) excluded: these have preserved or variable reflexes, different pattern of weakness, and diagnostic muscle biopsy findings; SMN1 testing normal

questions.domain: Non-5q SMA variants excluded — BICD2, DYNC1H1, TRPV4 (autosomal dominant SMA mimics) negative?
questions.question: Yes – dominant SMA-like conditions (BICD2-related motor neuron disease, DYNC1H1-related disorder) have dominant inheritance; often predominantly lower extremity; normal SMN1 copy number on standard testing

questions.domain: Congenital myasthenic syndrome excluded — no fatigable weakness, repetitive stimulation normal?
questions.question: Yes – CMS may present with infantile hypotonia but typically shows fatigable weakness, normal reflexes early, and response to pyridostigmine; SFEMG and neuromuscular junction panel distinguish from SMA

sections.heading:
Clinical History: No additional cost (obtained during patient encounter and parental interview)
Clinical Exam: No additional cost (neurological examination by clinician — tone, reflexes, tongue, facial expression, respiratory pattern assessment)
Medium: $50–1,500 (serum CK $50–150; pulmonary function testing / FVC $300–600; overnight pulse oximetry $200–500; spine X-ray $200–400; EMG/NCS $800–1,500; videofluoroscopic swallow study $500–1,000)
Large: $500–5,000+ (SMN1 exon 7 deletion analysis with SMN2 copy number $500–1,500; SMN1 full gene sequencing for intragenic mutations $1,000–2,500; parental carrier testing $500–2,000; muscle biopsy + histology $2,000–5,000)

Homozygous SMN1 exon 7 deletion confirmed (25 points) — DEFINITIVE DIAGNOSIS
Never achieved sitting independently OR sitter-never-walker milestone profile (12 points) — CARDINAL CLINICAL CLASSIFICATION FEATURE
Positive newborn screening result for SMA (12 points) — PRE-SYMPTOMATIC IDENTIFICATION
Symmetric progressive proximal muscle weakness (10 points) — ESSENTIAL CLINICAL FEATURE
Profound hypotonia / frog-leg resting posture (10 points) — HALLMARK INFANTILE PRESENTATION
Absent deep tendon reflexes / areflexia (10 points) — CARDINAL LOWER MOTOR NEURON SIGN
Visible tongue fasciculations (10 points) — PATHOGNOMONIC LOWER MOTOR NEURON SIGN
SMN2 copy number determined (8 points) — CRITICAL PROGNOSTIC AND TREATMENT-URGENCY MODIFIER
Pure lower motor neuron phenotype — no UMN signs (8 points) — ESSENTIAL DIAGNOSTIC CRITERION
Paradoxical breathing / bell-shaped chest / intercostal weakness (8 points) — TYPE 1 HALLMARK FEATURE
Chronic denervation pattern on EMG (8 points) — CONFIRMATORY ELECTRODIAGNOSTIC FINDING
Onset of hypotonia and weakness before 6 months of age (10 points) — TYPE 1 DEFINING ONSET WINDOW

Phase 1 — Clinical Evaluation (No Cost):
  • Comprehensive pregnancy and birth history — reduced fetal movements ("quiet baby") in ~30% of Type 1; assess kick count history
  • Detailed motor milestone history with parental demonstration (photographs or video if available)
  • Neurological examination: bulk, tone, reflexes, tongue fasciculations, facial expression, eye movements, paradoxical breathing
  • Functional motor assessment: head control, rolling, sitting, standing, hand-to-mouth, cry strength
  Potential: 50–70 points for $0

Phase 2 — Targeted Workup ($50–1,500):
  • Serum CK — normal/near-normal supports SMA; markedly elevated (>5–10× ULN) redirects to muscular dystrophy
  • Pulmonary function testing (FVC % predicted) if child cooperative; overnight pulse oximetry for nocturnal hypoventilation
  • EMG/NCS — confirm denervation pattern and normal conduction velocities (often deferred if SMN1 testing promptly ordered)
  Additional: 10–25 points for $50–1,500

Phase 3 — Definitive Genetic Testing ($500–2,500):
  • Step 1: SMN1 exon 7 copy number analysis by MLPA or ddPCR — with SMN2 copy number (same assay)
    → Homozygous deletion (0 copies SMN1): DIAGNOSTIC — initiate treatment workup immediately
    → Heterozygous (1 copy SMN1): Step 2 — SMN1 full gene sequencing for intragenic mutation on second allele
    → 2 copies SMN1: 5q SMA unlikely; consider non-5q SMA panel (BICD2, DYNC1H1) or neuromuscular panel
  • Parental carrier testing as needed for family planning or to clarify ambiguous proband results
  Additional: 25–40 points — crosses diagnostic threshold in virtually all true SMA cases

• TREATMENT IS TIME-CRITICAL — SMA is now a highly treatable disease with three FDA-approved therapies; earlier treatment = dramatically better outcomes; delay = irreversible motor neuron loss
• THREE APPROVED THERAPIES: (1) Spinraza/nusinersen (intrathecal ASO, Biogen) — approved for all SMA types, all ages, every 4 months; (2) Zolgensma/onasemnogene abeparvovec IV (one-time gene therapy, Novartis) — approved for patients <2 years; (3) Itvisma (intrathecal Zolgensma formulation, Novartis) — FDA approved November 2025 for patients ≥2 years, teens, and adults; (4) Evrysdi/risdiplam (oral SMN2 splicing modifier, Genentech) — approved from 2 months of age, home administration
• NEWBORN SCREENING — approved in 45+ US states and 25+ countries; NBS result available day 2–5 of life; positive result requires IMMEDIATE specialist referral; pre-symptomatic treatment yields near-normal motor development in many Type 1 genotypes
• SMN2 COPY NUMBER is the most critical genetic prognostic modifier: 1 copy → most severe (neonatal/Type 0); 2 copies → typical Type 1; 3 copies → Type 2; 4 copies → Type 3–4; must be determined at diagnosis for treatment urgency assessment
• COMPOUND HETEROZYGOSITY — ~5% of SMA patients have deletion on one SMN1 allele and a point mutation on the other; single-allele deletion on standard dosage testing does NOT rule out SMA; SMN1 full sequencing required in these cases
• SMN1 CARRIER FREQUENCY is ~1/40–50 in the general population; ACMG recommends universal carrier screening for all reproductive-age individuals; carrier testing by SMN1 dosage (MLPA/ddPCR) has ~95% sensitivity (2+0 carriers may be missed)
• RESPIRATORY MANAGEMENT is paramount — proactive NIV (BiPAP), mechanical insufflation-exsufflation (cough assist / MI-E), suction, and early airway clearance protocols save lives in Type 1–2; FVC <40% or nocturnal hypoventilation indicate NIV initiation
• This atlas entry covers 5q SMA (SMN1-related), the most common form; non-5q SMA (BICD2-related, DYNC1H1-related, X-linked SMA/Kennedy disease, distal SMA variants) are distinct entities requiring separate genetic evaluation
• MULTIDISCIPLINARY CARE is standard: neurology, pulmonology, gastroenterology/nutrition, orthopedics, physical/occupational/speech therapy, and palliative care as appropriate — SMA Certified Care Center designation (Cure SMA program) identifies specialized centers
SMA Clinical Type Classification and Phenotypic Spectrum

Type 0 (Prenatal / Neonatal Onset) — Most Severe:
  • Onset in utero — absent or severely reduced fetal movements; severe arthrogryposis at birth
  • Respiratory failure at birth; requires immediate ventilatory support; usually fatal within weeks without aggressive intervention
  • 1–2 SMN2 copies; most severe genotype

Type 1 (Werdnig-Hoffmann Disease) — Onset <6 Months; Never Sitter:
  • Classic "floppy infant"; frog-leg posture; paradoxical breathing; weak cry; tongue fasciculations; absent reflexes
  • Without treatment: median survival <2 years (respiratory failure); never achieves sitting
  • With disease-modifying therapy (pre-symptomatic): many achieve sitting, standing, and walking; dramatic improvement in survival
  • 2 SMN2 copies in most; ~60% of all SMA cases

Type 2 (Dubowitz Disease) — Onset 6–18 Months; Sitter, Never Walker:
  • Achieves independent sitting; never achieves independent standing or walking
  • Minipolymyoclonus; progressive scoliosis; respiratory involvement typically after age 10
  • 3 SMN2 copies in most; survival into adulthood with appropriate care; ~27% of SMA cases

Type 3 (Kugelberg-Welander Disease) — Onset >18 Months; Walker:
  • Achieves independent walking; may lose ambulation over years (Type 3a: loss before 3 years; Type 3b: loss after 3 years)
  • Proximal weakness; Gowers maneuver; waddling gait; CK may be mildly elevated; scoliosis less severe
  • 3–4 SMN2 copies; normal lifespan; ~12% of SMA cases

Type 4 (Adult-Onset SMA) — Onset >18–30 Years:
  • Slowly progressive proximal limb weakness in adulthood; mildly reduced lifespan; normal respiratory function at onset
  • 4+ SMN2 copies; often underdiagnosed; may be confused with limb-girdle muscular dystrophy

Key Differential Diagnoses:
  • Congenital Myopathies (nemaline, central core, centronuclear) — preserved reflexes; specific muscle biopsy / gene panel findings; SMN1 normal
  • Congenital Muscular Dystrophy (LAMA2/MDC1A, COL6A) — elevated CK; white matter MRI changes; muscle biopsy distinguishes
  • Pompe Disease / GSD II — hypotonia + cardiomegaly + elevated CK; acid glucosidase enzyme assay; now on NBS in many states
  • Prader-Willi Syndrome — neonatal hypotonia + dysmorphic features + hypogonadism; methylation study at 15q11.2-q13
  • Non-5q SMA (BICD2, DYNC1H1, TRPV4) — autosomal dominant; predominantly lower extremity; normal SMN1 copy number
  • Congenital Myasthenic Syndromes — fatigable weakness; variable reflexes; neuromuscular junction panel; response to pyridostigmine

confidenceNote:
🔴  85–100 points: High Confidence — SMA highly likely; proceed directly to SMN1 exon 7 deletion analysis and urgent treatment evaluation without delay
🟡  40–84 points: Moderate Confidence — SMA probable or possible; SMN1 genetic testing indicated urgently; do not defer genetic testing awaiting EMG if clinical picture is consistent; consider neuromuscular gene panel if SMN1 deletion is negative
🟢  <40 points: Low Confidence — 5q SMA less likely; broaden differential to congenital myopathy, congenital muscular dystrophy, Pompe disease, Prader-Willi syndrome, or hereditary neuropathy
